fields.expected:
Something that doesn't show up anywhere on my resume: I got a meeting with the president of Johns Hopkins by knocking on a locked door. During Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Daniels was nearby. We walked over to Garland Hall, saw him through the glass, and knocked until someone let us pitch ClarityAtlas. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute.

The other thing you won't find listed is how much time I spend on a question that has no deliverable attached. Over the past year I've been reading about how research gets funded and evaluated, from patronage to Bell Labs to the NIH project-grant model to newer structures like DARPA and Focused Research Organizations, and interviewing researchers, administrators, and science-policy people. I started out convinced grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. Talking to actual researchers changed that. I now think the bigger effect is selection: people learn which ideas are legible enough to get funded and quietly stop attempting the ones that aren't.

fields.expected: I work most with Python and PyTorch for modeling, plus XGBoost and SHAP for gradient-boosted models and interpretation on large survey data. On the LLM side I have built retrieval-augmented generation pipelines using OpenAI models and embeddings with Pinecone vector search and a Neo4j graph, rubric-driven LLM judging systems where separate judges score dimensions in parallel and then synthesize a cited assessment, and evaluation frameworks for AI-generated clinical outputs benchmarked against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling. I have also done temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style architectures for anomaly scoring, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and CNN training in PyTorch for facial-landmark prediction. Around the models, I serve things with FastAPI, and for agent work I use TypeScript, Node, and Playwright with explicit state machines, Zod validation, and fail-closed flags so LLM calls stay at narrow, reviewable call sites.
